config.title: Concurrent Mode Gotchas

intro.title: Concurrent Mode Gotchas
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React app to understand common pitfalls when using Concurrent Mode. You'll learn how Concurrent Mode can cause unexpected behavior in components that rely on synchronous state updates or external data. The core concepts covered include state management, side effects, and React's rendering lifecycle. You'll use React hooks like useState and useEffect, and work with JSX to create the user interface. This hands-on exercise will help you write more predictable and efficient React applications.
intro.usecase: Concurrent Mode is crucial for building responsive, high-performance applications like live dashboards, real-time collaboration tools, or complex e-commerce product filters. For example, when a user interacts with a large data table—sorting columns while new data streams in—Concurrent Mode ensures the UI remains interactive, preventing janky rendering or input lag. Developers implementing features such as background data fetching during route transitions or prioritizing urgent UI updates (like a typing indicator) over less critical ones rely on these patterns to deliver a seamless user experience.

objectives: Implement Suspense boundaries to handle loading states in Concurrent Mode
Apply useTransition hook to manage non-urgent state updates
Configure useDeferredValue to defer rendering of non-critical UI updates
Update component structures to prevent tearing during concurrent renders
Initialize and control concurrent features with startTransition API
Manipulate component lifecycle to avoid race conditions in Concurrent Mode
Integrate error boundaries with Suspense to handle component failures gracefully

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported, making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns JSX containing a single <div> element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component is defined and returns an empty div.
successCriteria: A functional component named App exists and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main App component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have a component named App that returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Create a function named App that returns a <div>.

steps.title: Initialize state for a counter
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare a state variable named 'count' with an initial value of 0 using useState.
steps.hint: Call useState(0) and destructure the returned array to get count and setCount.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: declaring a state variable
const [value, setValue] = useState('initial');
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'count' initialized to 0, ready to demonstrate concurrent rendering behavior.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with 0, and the returned array is destructured into count and setCount.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with an initial value of 0 and destructuring the array into count and setCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the useState hook inside your component to create a state variable called 'count' starting at 0.

steps.title: Initialize state for a loading indicator
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, declare a second state variable named 'isLoading' with an initial value of false using useState.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create another state variable. Place it after the existing count state declaration.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding another state variable
const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: count and isLoading.
successCriteria: The App component contains a state variable named 'isLoading' initialized to false using useState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState to declare a variable named 'isLoading' with initial value false.
steps.feedbackWrong: declare a state variable named 'isLoading' with an initial value of false using useState.

steps.title: Create a slow increment handler
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a function called handleSlowIncrement that updates the count state after a simulated delay.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses setTimeout to delay the state update. Use the setCount function from useState to increment the count after the delay.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named handleSlowIncrement is defined inside the App component that uses setTimeout to increment the count state after a delay.
successCriteria: The handleSlowIncrement function is defined, uses setTimeout, and calls setCount to update the state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function uses setTimeout and properly updates the count state using setCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function called handleSlowIncrement that delays the state update using setTimeout.

steps.title: Create a fast increment handler
steps.instruction: Create a function called handleFastIncrement that updates the count state immediately by incrementing it by 1.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses the setCount updater to increase count by 1. This handler will be used to demonstrate immediate state updates.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a handleFastIncrement function that directly updates the count state, contrasting with the delayed update in handleSlowIncrement.
successCriteria: The handleFastIncrement function is defined and uses setCount to increment count by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your handleFastIncrement function uses setCount to update the count state by adding 1 to its current value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function named handleFastIncrement that updates the count state by incrementing it by 1 using setCount.

steps.title: Add the count display
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value.
steps.hint:
Use JSX to create a

element with the count state variable inside curly braces.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a state value in JSX

Current value: {someState}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: A paragraph element displays the current count value using JSX interpolation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the count variable inside the paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element isn't displaying the count value correctly. Check that you're using the count variable inside curly braces.

steps.title: Add the slow increment button and wire its onClick
steps.instruction: In the return statement of your App component, add a button element with the text 'Slow Increment' and set its onClick handler to call the handleSlowIncrement function.
steps.hint: Place the button inside the fragment (<>...</>) after the existing paragraph. Use the onClick attribute to connect it to your handler function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a button with an onClick handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click Me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Slow Increment' appears in the UI, which when clicked triggers the slow increment handler.
successCriteria: A button element with text 'Slow Increment' is added to the return statement, and its onClick attribute is set to handleSlowIncrement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it has the correct text and onClick handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly connected to the handler. Check the button's text and onClick attribute.

steps.title: Add the fast increment button and wire its onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Fast Increment' and wire its onClick event to call the handleFastIncrement function.
steps.hint: Place the button after the existing slow increment button. Use the onClick prop to call the handler function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: adding a button with an onClick handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Fast Increment' appears in the UI, and clicking it triggers the handleFastIncrement function.
successCriteria: The button element with text 'Fast Increment' is added, and its onClick prop is set to handleFastIncrement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it calls handleFastIncrement when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button or its onClick handler is missing or incorrect. Check the button text and the handler function name.

steps.title: Add loading indicator display
steps.instruction: Add conditional rendering inside the component's return statement to display 'Loading...' when the loading state is true.
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator or logical AND operator to conditionally render text based on the loading state value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show 'Loading...' text when the loading state is true, providing visual feedback during the slow increment operation.
successCriteria: Conditional rendering is added to display 'Loading...' text when loading state is true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're conditionally rendering text based on the loading state. Check that you're using the correct state variable name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading indicator isn't properly implemented. Remember to add conditional rendering that displays 'Loading...' when the loading state is true.
